pages.text:
HIGH COURT OF JUDICATURE AT ALLAHABAD
APPLICATION U/S 482 No. 8921 of 2023

Ramesh Chand and Another ...Applicants
Versus
State of U.P. and Another ...Opposite Parties

Counsel for Applicants: Sri Rajiv Lochan Shukla
Counsel for Opposite Parties: G.A., Sri Vikas Agarwal

Hon'ble Rahul Chaturvedi, J.

Heard learned counsel for applicants and learned counsel for opposite party no. 2. The present application under Section 482 Cr.P.C. has been filed for quashing the charge sheet in Case Crime No. 214 of 2022 under Sections 420, 406 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code, Police Station Kotwali, District Mathura.

1. The background of the present application reveals that opposite party no. 2 lodged an FIR on 14th June 2022 alleging that the applicants entered into an agreement for supply of industrial timber and received an advance of Rs. 18,50,000/- but failed to supply the full consignment.

2. On the basis of the said FIR, the police conducted investigation and submitted a chargesheet against the applicants for offences punishable under Section 420 (Cheating), Section 406 (Criminal breach of trust), and Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code.
3. Learned counsel for the applicants submitted that the dispute between the parties is purely civil and commercial in nature arising out of a written supply agreement dated 10th January 2021.
4. It was urged that part consignment worth Rs. 11,20,000/- was duly supplied and received by the complainant, as acknowledged in the delivery challans annexed with the application.
5. The remaining supply was delayed due to market fluctuations and supply chain disruptions during the pandemic, which gives rise to a contractual breach but not a criminal offence.

6. Counsel placed reliance on the landmark judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal, 1992 Supp (1) SCC 335, wherein it was held that criminal proceedings instituted with an ulterior motive must be quashed.

7. In response, learned Additional Government Advocate and learned counsel for opposite party no. 2 submitted that the applicants had dishonest intention from the very beginning and misappropriated the advance money.

8. Learned counsel for opposite party no. 2 argued that disputed questions of fact cannot be adjudicated in proceedings under Section 482 CrPC and the applicants must stand trial before the learned Magistrate.

9. This Court has considered the submissions and examined the materials on record. To constitute an offence of cheating under Section 420 IPC, there must be fraudulent or dishonest intention at the time of making the initial promise.
10. As held by the Apex Court in Hridaya Ranjan Prasad Verma v. State of Bihar (2000) 4 SCC 168, a mere failure to keep a promise at a subsequent stage cannot be equated with criminal cheating.

11. Similarly, for an offence of criminal breach of trust under Section 406 IPC, there must be entrustment of property and dishonest misappropriation. The two offences of Section 420 and Section 406 IPC are mutually antithetical in standard commercial dealings.

12. In Paramjit Batra v. State of Uttarakhand (2013) 11 SCC 673, the Supreme Court cautioned that courts must see whether a dispute which is essentially of a civil nature is given a cloak of criminal offence.

14. The dispute is purely commercial arising out of breach of a business contract. A mere breach of contract cannot give rise to criminal prosecution for cheating under Section 420 IPC unless dishonest intention is present from the inception.
15. In the result, the application under Section 482 Cr.P.C. is allowed. The impugned charge sheet and entire criminal proceedings against the applicants stand quashed.

record.summary: The Allahabad High Court quashed criminal proceedings instituted under Sections 420, 406, and 34 of the IPC against the applicants. The Court held that the dispute was civil and commercial in nature, and failure to honor a contract cannot be converted into a criminal offence of cheating without fraudulent intent at inception.
record.summary_hi: इलाहाबाद हाईकोर्ट ने धारा 420, 406 और 34 आईपीसी के तहत दर्ज आपराधिक मामले को रद्द कर दिया। अदालत ने कहा कि व्यापारिक अनुबंध के उल्लंघन का विवाद दीवानी प्रकृति का है और इसे धोखाधड़ी का आपराधिक मामला नहीं बनाया जा सकता।

brief.facts: An FIR was lodged against the applicants under IPC Sections 420, 406 alleging non-delivery of textiles after receiving advance payment under a commercial supply agreement.
issues: Whether breach of commercial contract constitutes the criminal offence of cheating under Section 420 IPC without dishonest intention from inception?
brief.arguments: Applicants submitted that the dispute was purely civil arising from commercial reconciliation. State contended that charge-sheet was submitted after investigation.
brief.reasoning: Every breach of contract does not give rise to criminal prosecution. Fraudulent intention must be shown at the very beginning of the transaction.
brief.decision: Section 482 application allowed. Criminal proceedings and charge sheet quashed.
